Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-09-03 14:30 PDT
- Duration: ~47 minutes
- Attendees: Avery Kim (Redwood AE), Diego Martiínez (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (NexaHealth ML Lead), Ethan Lowe (NexaHealth Platform), Marta Novak (NexaHealth CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood and NexaHealth scoped a POC focused on chat inference SLOs. Primary topics: define TTFT vs TPOT targets, choose p95/p99 thresholds, workload sizing (concurrency, typical prompt lengths and percentiles), and measurement plan (replay vs synthetic, warm vs cold, metrics to collect). Action items and next steps captured.

Topics covered:
- Definitions: TTFT and TPOT and how Redwood measures them
- Success criteria: p95/p99 latency targets, throughput (tokens/s) and availability
- Workload sizing: typical prompt length, batch sizes, concurrency, peak vs baseline
- Benchmark plan: replayed traffic, synthetic load, warm-cache vs cold-start
- Timeline and acceptance criteria for POC

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros? We have about 45 minutes so we'll try to get SLOs, workload numbers and a measurement approach nailed down.
[00:09] Priya Shah: Thanks, Avery. Priya here. Our ML team owns the chat assistant model infra. Mostly interactive user queries, some longer context threads.
[00:15] Marta Novak: Marta - CTO. Focus is reliability and data residency, want clear success criteria.
[00:20] Ethan Lowe: Ethan - platform. I care about network, VPC and keys.
[00:24] Diego Martiínez: Hi everyone, Diego from Redwood infra team. I'll own the benchmark harness and run the initial pilots.
[00:31] Avery: Great. Quick context from Nexa - Priya, can you describe traffic shape? Percentile of prompt lengths, average tokens in completions, and concurrent users?
[00:45] Priya: Yeah so typical sessions are 1-3 messages per user. Prompt token distribution - median around 80 tokens, p95 ~420 tokens, p99 ~900 tokens. Completion lengths vary, median completions ~60 tokens but heavy tail to ~700 tokens on rare cases. Concurrency during peak is roughly 380 concurrent active sessions, but our front end multiplexes some requests so request concurrency hitting model tends to be around 220.
[01:12] Diego: Helpful. So when we talk about TTFT vs TPOT for this workload, quick definition from Redwood side - TTFT is time-to-first-token measured from request ingress to first token emitted by the model. TPOT in our internal shorthand is time-per-token or tokens-per-second depending on context; we should pick consistent metric - we'll treat TPOT as tokens/sec throughput for steady-state reporting and also measure per-token latency for long sequences.
[01:36] Priya: Makes sense. For SLOs we care most about TTFT for user perceived latency and tokens/sec for throughput so UX doesn't stutter mid-response.
[01:44] Avery: Exactly. For reference, our hosted customers usually aim for TTFT p95 120-200ms for short prompt path, p99 under 400-500ms. But that's with smaller models, heavy quantization and aggressive batching. For mid-sized Llama-style models or production tuned models with KV cache, we can often hit p95 ~250ms and p99 ~600ms depending on sequence length and batching.
[02:14] Marta: We're more conservative given healthcare workflows. We want p95 TTFT under 300ms for prompts under 200 tokens and p99 under 900ms across all traffic. Is that realistic?
[02:26] Diego: It's plausible. We need to define the test cases: short prompts (<200 tokens), medium (200-500), and long (>500). For short prompts under 200 tokens your targets map to p95 250-300ms, p99 700-900ms. But you'll see TTFT degrade with cold-starts and if we enable larger batch windows.
[02:46] Priya: Cold starts - we care about tail because sporadic long-running threads are more sensitive. How do you measure cold vs warm?
[02:54] Diego: We'll do two passes: 1) cold-run simulation where model VMs are idle for 15-30 minutes then we replay bursts; 2) steady-state run where we warm KV caches and run for 1-2 hours at target concurrency. We'll capture TTFT p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. Also measure first-byte latency variability during cache misses.
[03:20] Avery: A couple of practical questions: what's your target throughput in tokens/sec during peak? Priya?
[03:27] Priya: Peak we'd like to sustain ~18k tokens/s end-to-end. That's about 20k including overhead, so let's say 20k tokens/s. But important is per-request latency, not just aggregate tokens.
[03:38] Diego: 20k tokens/s is a helpful goal. We'll size the pilot to a dedicated pool that can sustain that with headroom for 25% spikes. We'll also record model utilization and GPU memory pressure.
[03:50] Ethan: On infra side, we'll likely run Redwood Private in our VPC for the POC. We need to confirm networking and KMS - is the plan to use customer-managed KMS?
[03:59] Avery: Yes we can support customer KMS/HSM for Private, and VPC peering or private link. Diego: we'll need a small set of firewall rules and egress allowed to our control plane (or air-gapped option if required).
[04:14] Marta: Compliance note - we need SOC2 artifacts and audit logs available for the POC.
[04:19] Avery: We'll attach our SOC2 report and the audit log configuration doc.
[04:23] Priya: Back to SLOs - we also want to define success criteria for quality regressions. Can we tie evaluation to a small prompt set so we can detect output changes when we switch model variants?
[04:33] Diego: Absolutely. Part of the benchmark harness is to run per-prompt scoring and check for hallucination/response quality regressions against a reference set. We'll include a golden set of 250 prompts that you give us to run diff-based metrics and a few human checks.
[04:46] Priya: Good. Now measurement specifics: windows, percentiles and sample sizes. We want p95 and p99 measured over rolling 1-hour windows but also an aggregate 24-hour percentile.
[04:56] Diego: That works. We'll compute p50/p90/p95/p99 for both TTFT and per-token latency, and tokens-per-second per-minute buckets. Recommended thresholds: for short prompt class: TTFT p95 < 300ms, p99 < 700ms; for medium: p95 < 500ms, p99 < 1200ms; for long: p95 < 900ms, p99 < 2000ms. These are starting points we can tune.
[05:22] Marta: Can we set a spillover policy - if p95 breaches, automatically route to a smaller model or different region?
[05:29] Diego: Yes Redwood supports policy routing and model fallback. For the POC we'll test fallbacks: fallback to a smaller quantized variant when latency SLOs breach, and verify quality delta with the golden set.
[05:41] Priya: How do you simulate real user behavior? Synthetic patterns often miss conversational context, e.g., back-and-forth threads.
[05:49] Diego: We prefer a hybrid approach: replay anonymized production traces (best) + synthetic stress tests for specific edge cases (long tails, bursty concurrency). Replay keeps conversation threading and true prompt distribution. Synthetic tests let us push to extremes.
[06:03] Ethan: We'll need instructions for anonymizing traces - remove PII and token-level content if necessary, but keep token lengths and inter-arrival timing.
[06:12] Avery: We'll provide a template for the trace export and a script that hashes or strips content while preserving lengths and timing.
[06:18] Priya: About metrics instrumentation - what labels do you expose? We want request_id, model_variant, shard_id, region, cache_hit boolean, and GPU_util.
[06:29] Diego: We'll expose all of that via metrics and logs. Metrics will be Prom-compatible counters/histograms; we'll house a short dashboard for p95 TTFT and TPOT and token throughput. We'll also ship sample Grafana dashboards.
[06:40] Priya: On measurement, how do you define warm KB caches? I heard KV cache but sometimes transcribed oddly as K V cash in previous notes.
[06:48] Diego: (laughs) Yeah transcription. KV cache means the model key-value cache for autoregressive decoding. Warm means the session has been recently served on the same shard so cache is populated. We'll do tests with 0/50/95% cache hit ratios.
[06:58] Marta: Any expectations on batch sizes? Our frontend tends to send single-request per user, but Redwood can batch within the runtime.
[07:06] Diego: We'll control batching behavior. For low-latency SLOs we recommend small micro-batches (1-4) and shorter batch windows (10-20ms). For cost-focused runs you can increase to 16-32. Part of the POC is evaluating cost vs latency tradeoffs.
[07:22] Avery: Let's capture explicit POC acceptance criteria. My suggestion and you can modify: 1) TTFT p95 < 300ms for short prompts, p99 < 900ms overall; 2) sustain average 20k tokens/s steady-state with <10% variance in 1-hour windows; 3) fallback behavior verified with <10% quality regression on the golden set; 4) security/compliance docs received.
[07:48] Priya: I like that. Add requirement that end-to-end from frontend to first token is measured including network egress from our VPC.
[07:56] Avery: Noted. We'll instrument from ingress to first token.
[07:59] Ethan: Timeline - what's a realistic cadence? We want to move quickly, two weeks for initial data handoff and harness prep, one week to run initial benchmarks, then refinements. So total 4 weeks?
[08:09] Diego: Timeline we typically do: week 0: data & infra prep; week 1: initial runs and cold vs warm; week 2: stress runs and fallbacks; week 3: final acceptance and report. So ~3-4 weeks depending on scheduling.
[08:24] Marta: That works. Cost question: how do you estimate GPU hours for the pilot?
[08:30] Diego: Based on your token budget and sequence lengths, we estimate ~180 GPU-hours for the dedicated pilot runs including warmups and multiple variants. We'll refine after we see the traces.
[08:40] Priya: Acceptable. One more - how do you measure p99 in presence of noise? Do you sample or use full traffic?
[08:46] Diego: We'll compute p99 from full capture during test windows. For production-like noisy traces we'll run multiple windows and present distribution of p99 across 1-hr windows to avoid single-blip bias.
[08:58] Avery: Ok let's log a few concrete test scenarios for Diego to run:
- Short prompt steady-state: 220 concurrency, median prompt 80 tokens, median completion 60 tokens, target 20k tokens/s, warm cache. 60-minute run.
- Medium prompt burst: 1-minute spike to 400 concurrency, prompts 250-400 tokens, measure TTFT p95/p99 and max queueing latency.
- Long tail validation: 10% of requests >500 tokens, single-hour run to validate tokens/sec and per-token latency.
- Cold-start window: idle 30 min then 15-minute replay at 100% peak traffic to measure cold TTFT.

[09:26] Priya: I like that. Please also include the golden quality set run after any fallback to measure regression.
[09:31] Diego: Will do. We'll produce a runbook with exact commands and expected outputs.
[09:37] Priya: For acceptance, who signs off? Likely Priya + Marta?
[09:40] Marta: Yes, Priya and I will sign off, plus platform if needed.
[09:44] Avery: Great. Recap next steps: Avery sends SLO doc + pricing by 2025-09-05; Diego shares harness and runbook by 2025-09-08; Nexa provides trace export by 2025-09-10; kick-off pilot run week of 2025-09-15.
[09:58] Ethan: We'll confirm VPC/KMS details by 2025-09-09.
[10:02] Priya: One quick clarification on metrics - we also want per-prompt QA labels and a small sample for human review after each run.
[10:09] Diego: We'll add that to the harness - human sampling + automated diffs.
[10:13] Avery: Perfect. Anything else?
[10:15] Marta: No, thanks. Looking forward to the run.
[10:17] Priya: Thanks all.
[10:18] Avery: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with artifacts.
